lead: An electrical actuator turns current into motion. A solenoid pushes a plunger a short straight distance. A relay uses that push to open or close contacts, so a small coil signal can switch a large load. A motor turns current into continuous rotation. These three cover most on-off and drive jobs in machines: a washing-machine inlet valve, a relay board switching a pump, a 12 V motor driving a robot wheel. This chapter gives the ratings, the force and speed relations, and the numbers an exam question asks for.
prereq: You need magnetic circuits and inductance for how a coil builds flux and how a moving plunger changes inductance, and pneumatic and hydraulic actuators to compare electrical actuators with fluid power.

blocks.text: A solenoid is a coil wound on a tube with a soft-iron plunger inside. Current in the coil makes a magnetic field, and the field pulls the plunger into the coil against a spring. The stroke is short, a few millimetres up to about 10 cm. Force is largest when the plunger is nearly seated and the air gap is small; it falls as the gap opens and the plunger is drawn out. This is the force-stroke curve. Pull-in must be strong enough at the open gap, and once seated a smaller hold current gives the same holding force. Design from the working point on the curve, not from the peak value.

The coil is a resistor with inductance. Pull-in current is the current needed to move the plunger and its load. Hold current is smaller: it only keeps the plunger seated. Many drivers apply full voltage for a moment, then drop to a lower hold voltage, so the coil runs cooler. Duty cycle is on time divided by total cycle time, in per cent. A solenoid rated 10% duty cycle must rest between pulses, or the coil overheats and the insulation fails. Uses: door locks, fuel injectors, washing-machine inlet valves, and in hospitals the pinch valves of dialysis machines and the gas valves of ventilators.

blocks.where: P is coil heating in watts; I is coil current in amperes; R is coil resistance in ohms; t<sub>on</sub> is the on time in seconds; T is the total cycle time in seconds.

sections.h3: Relay: coil on one side, contacts on the other

blocks.text: A relay is a solenoid plus a set of contacts. The coil pulls an armature; the armature carries a moving contact that touches a fixed contact. A spring returns it when the coil is off.

A relay has two independent ratings. The coil rating is the voltage and power needed to work it: a 24 V coil of 480 Ω draws 0.05 A and dissipates 1.2 W. The contact rating is the current and voltage the contacts may switch, say 10 A at 250 V AC. A 24 V coil says nothing about whether those contacts can break a 230 V mains pump. Check both.

Contacts come as normally open (NO, closed only when the coil is energised) and normally closed (NC, closed when the coil is off). The common terminal is the moving contact. A solid-state relay (SSR) replaces the coil-armature-contact assembly with an LED that shines on a light-sensitive triac. The LED is the input, the triac is the output switch, and the light couples them with no moving parts. A triac is two thyristors back to back, so it conducts on both half-cycles of AC. No contacts wear, switching is fast and silent, but the triac drops about 1 V, needs a heat sink, and leaks a small current when off.

sections.h3: DC motor: back emf sets the speed

blocks.text: A DC motor has a magnetic field (from a winding or from permanent magnets) and an armature carrying current. Armature current flowing in the magnetic field (flux) produces torque. As the armature turns it cuts flux and generates a back emf that opposes the supply. At steady state:

blocks.where: Eb is back emf in volts; V is supply voltage in volts; Ia is armature current in amperes; Ra is armature resistance in ohms; T is torque in newton metres; φ is flux per pole in webers; k is a motor constant.

blocks.text: Back emf is also proportional to speed, Eb = kφω with ω in rad/s, so speed ≈ (V − IaRa) ÷ (kφ). Speed rises almost in proportion to applied voltage. Torque rises in proportion to armature current. At standstill Eb = 0, so Ia = V ÷ Ra, several times the full-load current; large DC motors need a starter. Types: shunt (field in parallel, nearly constant speed), series (field in series, high starting torque, never run unloaded), permanent-magnet (small, cheap, used in car wipers, robot wheels and the infusion and syringe pumps of a hospital ward).

A three-phase induction motor has three stator windings fed 120° apart. Their currents make a field rotating at synchronous speed Ns = 120f ÷ P, where Ns is in revolutions per minute, f is supply frequency in hertz and P is the number of poles. The rotating field induces currents in the rotor cage, and the rotor is dragged along a little slower than the field.

blocks.where: s is slip, a pure number; Ns is synchronous speed in rpm; Nr is rotor speed in rpm.

blocks.text: Slip is 1 at standstill and a few per cent at full load, typically 2% to 5%. Torque rises with slip up to a breakdown value, then falls. At start the rotor is stationary, slip is 1, and the rotor behaves like a short-circuited transformer: starting current is 5 to 8 times full-load current while starting torque is only about 1.5 to 2 times full load. Star-delta starters, soft starters and variable-frequency drives limit this current. A synchronous motor turns exactly at Ns: its rotor, permanent-magnet or DC-fed, locks to the rotating field. It has no slip, so it suits clocks and precise drives, but it has no starting torque of its own.

spec.aria: Equivalent circuit of a DC motor: a 12 volt cell, armature resistance 1 ohm and a motor of back emf 10 volts carrying 2 amperes; a power flow from 24 watts in through 20 watts converted to 18 watts at the shaft with 4 and 2 watt losses; below, a coil current trace stepping to 2.0 amperes, down to 0.5 amperes, then off until 20 seconds.

examples.question: A permanent-magnet DC motor runs from a 12 V supply and draws 2 A at full load. Its armature resistance is 1 Ω. The shaft delivers 18 W. Find (a) the electrical input power, (b) the back emf, (c) the efficiency.
steps: Input power: Pin = V × Ia = 12 V × 2 A = 24 W.
Armature resistance drop: IaRa = 2 A × 1 Ω = 2 V.
Back emf: Eb = V − IaRa = 12 V − 2 V = 10 V.
Copper loss in the armature: Ia²Ra = 2² × 1 = 4 W. So 24 W − 4 W = 20 W becomes mechanical power.
Of that 20 W, 18 W leaves the shaft; the remaining 2 W is friction, windage and iron loss.
Efficiency: η = Pout ÷ Pin = 18 W ÷ 24 W = 0.75, that is 75%.
examples.answer: Input power 24 W, back emf 10 V, efficiency 75%.
examples.check:
V = 12.0
Ia = 2.0
Ra = 1.0
Pout = 18.0
Pin = V * Ia
Eb = V - Ia * Ra
eta = Pout / Pin
print(Pin)
print(Eb)
print(eta)

examples.question: A 24 V solenoid valve has a coil resistance of 12 Ω. Its driver applies 24 V to pull in, then drops to 6 V to hold. The valve is energised for 2 s in every 20 s. Find (a) the pull-in current and power, (b) the hold current and power, and (c) the duty cycle and the average power if it were held at 24 V.
steps: (b) Hold: I = 6 / 12 = 0.5 A; P = I²R = 0.5² × 12 = 3.0 W, one sixteenth of the pull-in power, because power goes as V².
(c) Duty cycle = t<sub>on</sub> / T × 100 % = 2 / 20 × 100 % = 10 %. Held at 24 V the average power would be 0.10 × 48 = 4.8 W.
Check: with the peak-and-hold driver the coil runs at 3.0 W while on, far below 48 W, so the same coil could be held continuously without overheating.
examples.answer: Pull-in draws 2.0 A and 48 W, hold 0.5 A and 3.0 W; the duty cycle is 10 %, an average of 4.8 W without the hold stage.

traps: Coil rating is not contact rating. A 24 V coil may switch 230 V mains, so give both when asked for a relay's ratings.
At standstill a DC motor has Eb = 0, so Ia = V ÷ Ra. A 12 V motor with 1 Ω that draws 2 A at load draws 12 A at start; the supply and driver must survive that.
Hold current is not pull-in current. Holding needs less current, and running a 10% duty-cycle coil at pull-in current continuously burns it out.

quiz.q: State the two independent ratings of a relay.
quiz.a: The coil rating (coil voltage, and the coil current or power it needs) and the contact rating (the maximum current and voltage the contacts may switch).

quiz.q: Why is the hold current of a solenoid smaller than its pull-in current?
quiz.a: Pull-in must produce enough force to move the plunger against the spring and load while the air gap is large. Once seated the gap is small and the same flux needs less current, so a lower hold current keeps it in place and cuts I²R heating.

quiz.q: A relay coil is rated 24 V and has a resistance of 480 Ω. Find the coil current and the coil power.
A 4-pole three-phase induction motor runs from a 50 Hz supply at 1440 rpm. Find the synchronous speed and the slip.
The load torque on a shunt DC motor increases. Explain what happens to armature current, back emf and speed.
quiz.a: Torque is proportional to armature current, so Ia rises. The larger IaRa drop makes Eb = V − IaRa fall. Because Eb is proportional to speed, the speed falls until the motor's torque again equals the load torque; the drop in speed is small for a shunt motor.

beyond: Not for the exam. Solid-state relays and MOSFET or IGBT switches have replaced coil relays in machines that switch many times a minute. Search volts-per-hertz control and peak-and-hold drivers.
